summary: The article provides generally accurate information regarding mutual fund red flags and tax implications, with a few minor discrepancies in specific tax rates and effective dates for new regulations.

claims.claim: SEBI regulates the maximum expense ratio that can be charged, with new regulations effective April 1, 2026, introducing a Base Expense Ratio (BER) framework for greater transparency.
claims.note: SEBI's new expense framework, introducing the Base Expense Ratio (BER), is indeed effective from April 1, 2026.

claims.claim: For direct plans, the expense ratio is typically lower than regular plans, often 0.5% to 1% less, as they eliminate distributor commissions.
claims.note: Direct plans generally have lower expense ratios (0.5% to 1% less) due to the absence of distributor commissions.

claims.claim: For equity-oriented funds, Long Term Capital Gains (LTCG) over ₹1 lakh in a financial year are taxed at 10% without indexation if held for more than 12 months.
claims.note: LTCG on equity funds is taxed at 10% on gains exceeding ₹1.25 lakh (not ₹1 lakh) in a financial year, without indexation, if held for more than 12 months. The ₹1 lakh limit was increased to ₹1.25 lakh in Budget 2024.

claims.claim: Short Term Capital Gains (STCG) are taxed at 15% if held for less than 12 months.
claims.note: STCG on equity-oriented funds held for less than 12 months is taxed at a flat rate of 15% if Securities Transaction Tax (STT) has been paid.

claims.claim: For debt funds purchased on or after April 1, 2023, all gains are taxed at your income tax slab rate, irrespective of the holding period, and no indexation benefit is allowed.
claims.note: For debt mutual funds purchased on or after April 1, 2023, all gains are indeed taxed at the investor's income tax slab rate, without indexation benefits, regardless of the holding period.

article_title: Mutual Funds: 5 Red Flags Signalling Time to Exit
